claims.text: The post-annealing cooling protocol governs structural phase evolution in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Rapid quenching kinetically freezes a homogeneous high-entropy configuration in CoCrFeMnNi nanoalloys.
Rapid quenching suppresses diffusion-driven phase segregation in CoCrFeMnNi nanoalloys.
Rapid quenching suppresses grain-boundary enrichment in CoCrFeMnNi nanoalloys.
Preservation of the homogeneous configuration produces a stable nanocrystalline microstructure.
The quenched nanocrystalline microstructure resists oxidation during subsequent high-temperature exposure better than a slowly cooled microstructure.
The proposed controlled comparison anneals CoCrFeMnNi samples at 900°C under inert atmosphere and varies only the post-annealing cooling protocol between quenching and slow cooling.
Quenching is expected to retain a homogeneous, metastable nanocrystalline phase rather than allowing segregated phases to form.
Slow cooling can permit formation of a structurally heterogeneous or multiphase microstructure after high-temperature annealing.
Slow cooling enhances atomic mobility relative to quenching.
Enhanced atomic mobility during slow cooling causes chemical segregation and grain-boundary enrichment.
Grain-boundary enrichment provides nucleation sites for oxidation.
Quenched samples will have a finer and more homogeneous nanostructure than slowly cooled samples.
Quenched samples will have less grain-boundary segregation than slowly cooled samples.
Quenched samples will exhibit lower oxidation rates than slowly cooled samples.
The prediction is limited to CoCrFeMnNi nanoalloys annealed at 900°C under inert conditions, because changes in temperature, duration, or composition may produce different kinetic regimes.
Grain-boundary evolution unrelated to diffusion-controlled segregation could also affect stability.
A lack of differences in phase segregation, grain-boundary composition, and oxidation between quenched and slowly cooled controls would falsify the proposed kinetic-stabilization mechanism.
